whyItExists.problem: Selecting and reading elements is only half the story. Real apps need to create new elements on the fly (a new message in a chat, a new card in a list) and remove old ones without reloading the page.
whyItExists.solution: createElement creates a new element in memory. append and remove attach and detach it from the page. Forms collect user input — reading their values and preventing default submission is the foundation of every web form.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Building dynamic UIs: adding/removing list items, rendering fetched data, building forms programmatically, creating modal dialogs.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid heavy DOM manipulation for large lists — use a framework. Avoid innerHTML with user data (XSS risk).

explainModes.beginner: createElement makes a new HTML element in JavaScript. Once you set its text and classes, append() puts it on the page. remove() takes it off the page.
explainModes.simple: const el = document.createElement('div') creates a div element. Set el.textContent, el.className, el.id. Then parent.append(el) to add it. el.remove() to delete it. innerHTML sets an element's entire HTML content.
explainModes.standard: createElement + append is safer than innerHTML for dynamic content. insertBefore, prepend, before, after give fine control over position. Forms: read input values with input.value. Handle submit with addEventListener('submit', e => { e.preventDefault(); }) and FormData.
explainModes.technical: appendChild and insertBefore are the classic DOM methods. Modern code prefers append (accepts multiple nodes and strings), prepend, before, after, and replaceWith — these are more ergonomic. Use DocumentFragment to batch multiple DOM insertions into one reflow. cloneNode(true) deep-copies an element. MutationObserver watches for DOM changes.
explainModes.deepDive: The Template element (<template>) holds inert HTML that doesn't render until cloned: template.content.cloneNode(true). Used for repeating structures. Shadow DOM encapsulates styles and DOM for web components — the boundary between a component's internal DOM and the page's DOM. Custom Elements (customElements.define) let you create your own HTML elements with lifecycle callbacks.

questions.question: What does event.preventDefault() do on a form submit event?
options: Stops the page from reloading/navigating after submit
questions.explanation: By default, submitting a form navigates to a new URL (or reloads the page). preventDefault() stops this, letting JavaScript handle the data without a page reload.

questions.question: Why use DocumentFragment instead of appending each element directly?
options: DocumentFragment is the only way to append multiple elements
It batches all DOM insertions into a single reflow instead of one per element
Elements in a fragment are visible while being built
questions.explanation: Each DOM append can trigger a reflow (layout recalculation). A DocumentFragment lives outside the DOM, so appending to it causes no reflow. When you append the fragment, all its children are inserted in one operation.

faq.q: Is innerHTML safe for inserting content?
faq.a: Only if the content is static and not from user input. Never set innerHTML to user-provided text (from an input, URL, or API) — malicious HTML can inject scripts (XSS). For user content, use textContent. For dynamic HTML you control, innerHTML is fine.

faq.q: What is the difference between append() and appendChild()?
faq.a: appendChild() is the classic method — it takes only one Node. append() is modern — it accepts multiple nodes AND plain strings, and converts strings to text nodes automatically. Prefer append() in new code.
